reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: Characteristic features include a periorificial and acral dermatitis, diarrhoea, alopecia, impaired wound healing, and altered taste
In children it causes growth faltering, recurrent infection, and delayed sexual maturation
Acquired deficiency arises with malabsorption, high-phytate cereal-based diets, chronic diarrhoea, extensive burns, and prolonged unsupplemented parenteral nutrition
The inherited disorder acrodermatitis enteropathica reflects defective intestinal zinc absorption and presents in infancy
Zinc supplementation reduces the duration and severity of acute diarrhoea in young children, a key public health measure in India and other low-income settings
The rash can closely mimic other nutritional dermatoses and is often initially misdiagnosed
Serum zinc is an imperfect marker because it falls with inflammation and hypoalbuminaemia, so results need cautious interpretation
reference.pathophysiology: Zinc is a component or regulator of hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors and is essential for cell division, protein synthesis, immune function, and epithelial integrity. Deficiency therefore most affects rapidly dividing and metabolically active tissues, producing dermatitis, impaired wound healing, mucosal disease, immune dysfunction, and, in children, growth and developmental impairment. Dietary phytates in cereals and legumes bind zinc and reduce its absorption, while malabsorptive states, excess gastrointestinal or urinary losses, and increased demand in growth, pregnancy, and tissue repair contribute to negative balance.
additionalDifferentials: Other nutritional deficiency dermatoses (for example essential fatty acid or biotin deficiency)
Other causes of growth failure in children
additionalInvestigations: Serum zinc, interpreted alongside albumin and inflammatory markers
Assessment for malabsorption and chronic gastrointestinal losses
Dietary history focusing on cereal-based, high-phytate diets
Skin examination and biopsy if the diagnosis is uncertain
Evaluation for the inherited disorder in an infant with typical features
redFlags: Severe dermatitis with secondary infection or extensive skin breakdown
Failure to thrive with recurrent serious infection in a child
Severe or persistent diarrhoea with dehydration
Deficiency in a patient on prolonged parenteral nutrition without trace element supplementation
reference.prognosis: Both acquired and inherited deficiency respond well to zinc repletion, with rapid resolution of skin and gastrointestinal features; the inherited form requires lifelong supplementation.
pitfalls: Interpreting a low serum zinc without accounting for inflammation and low albumin
Mistaking the dermatitis for eczema or another primary skin disease
Forgetting trace element provision during long-term parenteral nutrition
Overlooking high dietary phytate as a cause of poor absorption
management: Correct the deficiency with oral zinc salt supplementation such as zinc sulphate or gluconate, which rapidly reverses the dermatitis, diarrhoea and taste disturbance
Treat the underlying cause, whether malabsorption, chronic gastrointestinal losses or burns, and add zinc to prolonged parenteral nutrition
Give dietary advice to increase bioavailable zinc and reduce the high-phytate cereal-based intake that impairs absorption
Provide lifelong zinc supplementation in the inherited disorder acrodermatitis enteropathica
Use adjunctive zinc supplementation in young children with acute diarrhoea to reduce its duration and severity
Monitor serum zinc, interpreted alongside albumin and inflammatory markers, and clinical response to guide dosing
Refer children with growth faltering, or an infant with typical inherited features, for specialist and genetic assessment
